title: Could Homework Widen the Gap Between Families?
paragraphs: Homework is so familiar to primary-school families that few people question it, yet a new paper from the University of Manchester argues that it may quietly widen educational inequality. The study, published in the British Journal of Sociology of Education, looks at how much time parents are expected to give to their children's schoolwork.

The authors follow a single case: a mother called Emma, who works until 8pm, and her child's teacher, Mrs Higgins. The first author was herself a parent at the school. Drawing on the ideas of the sociologist Pierre Bourdieu, the researchers treat parents' time as a kind of cultural capital. Families with more time, knowledge and money can support homework, or buy private tutoring, while others struggle. Dr Emilia Howker said: "Some parents simply have more time and resources available to them."

There is a further risk, the authors say: schools may interpret a lack of time as a lack of commitment, which can lead to a "deficit" view of some parents. Because the paper is based on one case, its conclusions cannot be generalised, and the press release does not report the study's funding. Professor Laura Black adds that scrapping homework would not be enough, since other forms of parental engagement could replace it; the bigger challenge, she says, is to rethink what schools expect from parents.

questions.q: What do the researchers mean by parents' time as cultural capital?
questions.a: Time is treated as a resource that gives some families an advantage.

questions.q: What risk do the authors see in how schools judge parents?
questions.a: Schools may read a lack of time as a lack of commitment.

questions.q: Why can the conclusions not be generalised?
questions.a: The paper is based on a single case.
